paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Most people think of soil as dirt: something to wash off hands and clothes. Yet a handful of healthy soil contains more living organisms than there are people on Earth. Bacteria, fungi, worms and insects form a complex community that recycles dead plants and animals into the nutrients that crops need. Without this hidden work, farming as we know it would be impossible.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The most important of these organisms may be fungi. Thin threads called hyphae spread through the soil and connect to plant roots, forming a partnership known as mycorrhiza. The fungus gains sugars from the plant, while the plant receives water and minerals that the fungus collects over a far larger area than roots could reach alone. Scientists estimate that about ninety per cent of land plants depend on this relationship.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Unfortunately, modern farming practices can damage this community. Repeated ploughing breaks up the fungal networks and exposes soil to the air, which speeds up the loss of carbon. Heavy use of chemical fertilisers can make plants less dependent on their fungal partners, so the partnership weakens. In some regions, the top layer of fertile soil has been reduced by half in a hundred and fifty years, and it can take five hundred years to form just two and a half centimetres of new soil.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: A growing number of farmers are changing their methods. In no-till farming, seeds are planted directly into last year's crop residue without ploughing. Cover crops, such as clover or rye, are grown between harvests to protect the surface and feed soil life. Early results are encouraging: farms using these methods often report better water retention and, after a few years, lower fertiliser costs. However, yields can fall during the transition, which discourages some farmers from trying.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The benefits go beyond farming. Healthy soil stores large amounts of carbon, and some scientists believe that improving soils worldwide could remove a significant share of the carbon dioxide produced by human activity. It would not replace the need to cut emissions, but it could help. As one researcher put it, we have spent a century studying the sky and ignoring the ground beneath our feet.
